What the original study did not say

Does it take 21 days to form a habit?

The figure came from a 1960s plastic surgeon. When it was measured, the average was 66 days, with great variation.

"It takes 21 days to form a habit" is repeated in self-help books and apps. The source seems to be the plastic surgeon Maxwell Maltz, who in his book Psycho-Cybernetics (1960) observed that his patients took a minimum of about 21 days to get used to their new face. Over time, "a minimum of about 21 days" became "21 days".

What Lally found

In 2010, Phillippa Lally and her team at University College London asked 96 people to choose a simple behaviour, such as drinking a glass of water with breakfast or going for a run before dinner, and repeat it daily for twelve weeks.

The time until the behaviour became automatic ranged from 18 to 254 days, with a median of 66. Missing the odd day did not derail the process. The practical conclusion: a habit usually takes longer than people say, and it is fine to slip up now and then.

References

  1. Lally, P. et al. (2010). How are habits formed: modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009.
  2. Maltz, M. (1960). Psycho-Cybernetics. Prentice-Hall.
